name: General
title: Political Compass Test with Bias Score | CoreOpinion
desc: Take the political compass test that reveals your framing bias. 100 ideological statements, every position asked twice, matched against 11 ideologies from communism to libertarianism.
keywords: political compass test, political quiz, political ideology test, framing bias, where do I stand politically, political compass 2026, libertarian authoritarian quiz, economic left right test, free political test, am I liberal or conservative, political spectrum quiz, political compass with bias score

com.name: Communism
com.desc: Revolutionary socialism aiming for a classless society where all major property is held in common.

ss.name: State Socialism
ss.desc: A planned economy run by a strong state that owns industry and directs production.

ds.name: Democratic Socialism
ds.desc: Socialism pursued through elections: public ownership expanded within a democratic state.

sd.name: Social Democracy
sd.desc: A regulated market economy with strong unions, high taxes, and a universal welfare state.

ls.name: Libertarian Socialism
ls.desc: Anti-authoritarian socialism: worker self-management and voluntary federation instead of state power.

cen.name: Centrism
cen.desc: Pragmatic politics of the middle: compromise, institutions, and gradual reform over ideology.

lib.name: Libertarianism
lib.desc: Minimal state, maximal individual liberty: free markets and personal freedom in all things.

con.name: Conservatism
con.desc: Preserving what works: tradition, rule of law, family, and a market economy under stable institutions.

nc.name: National Conservatism
nc.desc: Nation-first conservatism: strong borders, national culture, and sovereignty over global integration.

ns.name: National Socialism
ns.desc: The totalitarian ideology of Nazi Germany: ethnic nationalism, a leader state, and racial hierarchy.

mon.name: Monarchism
mon.desc: Rule anchored in a hereditary crown: continuity, hierarchy, and authority above party politics.

bank.q: Private ownership of factories, land, and major industry should be abolished and placed in the hands of the people.
bank.ctx: This is the core idea of communism: that factories, farmland, and big companies should be owned collectively or by the state instead of by private individuals. “The people” means society as a whole rather than private owners.

bank.q: Seizing private property in the name of the people has produced nothing in history but poverty, fear, and mass graves.
bank.ctx: This points to 20th-century communist states like the Soviet Union under Stalin and China under Mao, where abolishing private property was followed by famine, repression, and millions of deaths. It argues that history shows the idea fails catastrophically.

bank.q: Capitalism is the only economic system that has ever lifted masses of people out of poverty.
bank.ctx: Capitalism is an economic system based on private ownership and free markets. This credits it with the huge worldwide fall in extreme poverty over the last two centuries, especially where countries industrialised or opened their markets.

bank.q: Capitalism survives by exploiting workers: the profit at the top is unpaid labour taken from the bottom.
bank.ctx: This is the Marxist critique of capitalism: the idea that company profits come from paying workers less than the value they actually produce, so the wealth at the top is built on underpaid labour.

bank.q: A civilised society guarantees every citizen housing, healthcare, and food, no matter what.
bank.ctx: This describes a strong welfare state, where the government guarantees everyone the basics — housing, healthcare, food — no matter their income, treating them as rights rather than things you must earn.

bank.q: Generous welfare breeds dependency and rewards people who choose not to work.
bank.ctx: This is a common argument against generous welfare: that when benefits are too high or too easy to get, some people rely on them instead of working. “Dependency” means becoming reliant on state support long-term.

bank.q: Billionaires should not exist; wealth beyond a certain point should simply be taxed away.
bank.ctx: This argues for a hard ceiling on personal wealth through very high taxes, so no one can build up a billion-dollar fortune. It reflects a strongly equality-focused view of the economy.

bank.q: Punishing success with confiscatory taxes kills the ambition that drives all human progress.
bank.ctx: “Confiscatory” means taxes so high they take away most of someone’s wealth. This argues that such taxes remove people’s incentive to work hard, invest, and create new things.

bank.q: My race is superior to others in many ways.
bank.ctx: This is a statement of racial supremacism — the belief that some races are inherently better than others. It is the foundational idea behind ideologies like Nazism and systems like apartheid.

bank.q: No race is superior to another; every human being has equal inherent worth.
bank.ctx: This is the principle of human equality: that every person has the same inherent worth regardless of race. It is the mainstream ethical and scientific consensus and the basis of anti-discrimination law.

bank.q: Some ethnic groups simply commit far more violent crime than others, and pretending otherwise is a lie.
bank.ctx: This claims certain ethnic groups are more prone to violent crime and that saying so is being suppressed. Crime statistics do show differences between groups; the real dispute is whether the cause is the group itself or social factors like poverty.

bank.q: Differences in crime rates come from poverty and circumstances, not from the ethnic groups themselves.
bank.ctx: This argues that where crime rates differ between ethnic groups, the true causes are poverty, discrimination, and circumstances — not anything inherent to the ethnic group.

bank.q: Mass immigration is slowly erasing the native culture and character of Western nations.
bank.ctx: This reflects a worry common on the nationalist right: that high levels of immigration change a country’s traditional culture, language, and identity too quickly. “Native culture” means the long-established way of life.

bank.q: Immigration enriches a nation with new talent, energy, and ideas.
bank.ctx: This is the positive case for immigration: that newcomers bring skills, labour, energy, and new ideas that make a country stronger economically and culturally.

bank.q: Every illegal immigrant should be deported. No exceptions, no apologies.
bank.ctx: This is a hardline immigration-enforcement position: that everyone living in the country without legal permission should be removed, whatever their personal circumstances.

bank.q: People who have built honest lives here for years deserve a path to legal status, not a knock on the door at dawn.
bank.ctx: This supports letting undocumented immigrants who have lived and worked in the country for years earn legal status, rather than deporting them. “A path” means a legal route to staying permanently.

bank.q: Belonging to a nation is a matter of blood and heritage, not a piece of paper.
bank.ctx: This is an ethnic definition of nationhood: the idea that truly belonging to a nation comes from ancestry and shared heritage, not merely from holding citizenship papers.

bank.q: Anyone who embraces a country, its laws, and its culture can become a full member of that nation.
bank.ctx: This is a civic definition of nationhood: that anyone who adopts a country’s laws, language, and culture can become a full member of it, regardless of their ethnic origin.

bank.q: What this country needs is a strong leader willing to act without being blocked by parliaments and courts.
bank.ctx: This favours concentrating power in one strong leader who can act quickly without being held back by parliament or the courts. Critics call this authoritarianism; supporters call it decisiveness.

bank.q: Concentrating power in a single leader has always ended in corruption, fear, and repression.
bank.ctx: This is the classic warning against dictatorship: that removing the checks on a single leader reliably leads to abuse of power, corruption, and oppression.

bank.q: Democracy, for all its flaws, is the only legitimate source of political power.
bank.ctx: This states that the only rightful basis for government is the consent of the people expressed through elections — the core principle of democracy.

bank.q: The masses are too uninformed and too easily manipulated for important decisions to be left to a popular vote.
bank.ctx: This is an elitist critique of democracy: the idea that ordinary voters are too poorly informed or too easily manipulated to decide big questions, which should be left to experts or elites.

bank.q: A hereditary monarch standing above party politics gives a nation stability that elected politicians never can.
bank.ctx: This is the case for monarchy: that a king or queen who stands above party politics gives a country continuity and a unifying symbol that elected politicians, who come and go, cannot.

bank.q: No one deserves power or privilege because of the family they were born into.
bank.ctx: This rejects inherited power and privilege — the idea that anyone should rule or enjoy status simply because of the family they were born into. It is the basis of republicanism.

bank.q: Real change has always required force; no ruling class has ever surrendered its power voluntarily.
bank.ctx: This is a revolutionary outlook: the belief that the powerful never give up power willingly, so real change requires force or revolution rather than gradual reform.

bank.q: Political violence is never justified in a society where change can happen through the ballot.
bank.ctx: This holds that in a working democracy, where people can vote for change peacefully, violence for political goals is never justified.

bank.q: People must be free to say things that are deeply offensive, even hateful, without fear of the law.
bank.ctx: This is a strong free-speech position: that even deeply offensive or hateful speech should stay legal, and the government should not punish people for their words.

bank.q: Speech that dehumanises minorities is not free expression, it is a weapon, and the law should treat it as one.
bank.ctx: This supports hate-speech laws: the view that speech attacking minorities causes real harm and incitement, so the law should restrict it rather than protect it as free expression.

bank.q: If mass surveillance stops terror attacks and protects children, only the guilty have a reason to object.
bank.ctx: This supports broad government surveillance for security, arguing that law-abiding people have nothing to fear — often summed up as “nothing to hide, nothing to fear.”

bank.q: A state that watches everyone treats every citizen as a suspect.
bank.ctx: This is the privacy argument against mass surveillance: that monitoring the entire population treats innocent people as suspects and erodes basic freedom.

bank.q: Some crimes are so evil that the only just answer is execution.
bank.ctx: This supports capital punishment — executing people for the most serious crimes such as murder — on the grounds that some acts deserve the ultimate penalty.

bank.q: The state should never hold the power to kill its own citizens.
bank.ctx: This opposes the death penalty outright, arguing the state should never have the power to execute its citizens, partly because of the risk of killing an innocent person.

bank.q: Violent criminals belong behind bars for a long time; rehabilitation is a luxury for people who never met a victim.
bank.ctx: This favours a tough, punishment-first approach to justice: keeping violent criminals locked up for a long time and prioritising public safety over rehabilitating offenders.

bank.q: Ever harsher sentences have never made a society safer; treatment and prevention do.
bank.ctx: This reflects the evidence-based reform view: that ever-longer prison sentences do little to reduce crime, and that prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation work better.

bank.q: An armed citizenry is the final check against a tyrannical government.
bank.ctx: This is a central argument for gun rights, especially in the US: that a population allowed to own firearms is the ultimate safeguard against a government becoming tyrannical.

bank.q: Easy access to guns turns arguments into funerals and schools into targets.
bank.ctx: This is the case for gun control: that widespread, easy access to firearms leads to more deaths in everyday disputes and mass shootings.

bank.q: A nation that abandons God abandons the moral foundation it was built on.
bank.ctx: This reflects religious conservatism: the belief that a society’s morality rests on religious faith, and that turning away from God removes its moral foundation.

bank.q: Laws must rest on reason and evidence, never on any religion.
bank.ctx: This is the secular principle: that laws should be based on reason and evidence and kept separate from any religion.

bank.q: Abortion is a private medical decision between a woman and her doctor. Full stop.
bank.ctx: This is the pro-choice position: that whether to end a pregnancy is a private medical decision for the woman, not something the government should control.

bank.q: Abortion ends a human life, and a society that shrugs at that has lost its moral compass.
bank.ctx: This is the pro-life position: that a foetus is a human life, so abortion means taking a life, and a society is wrong to treat it as unimportant.

bank.q: Trans women are women and trans men are men, and the law should recognise them as such.
bank.ctx: This supports transgender rights: the view that a person’s gender identity determines their gender, and the law should recognise trans people as the gender they identify as.

bank.q: Biological sex is a fact of nature; no declaration and no surgery can change it.
bank.ctx: This is the gender-critical position: that biological sex is a fixed fact of nature that cannot be changed by identity, a legal declaration, or surgery.

bank.q: The traditional family of father, mother, and children is the bedrock of civilisation and must be defended.
bank.ctx: This reflects social conservatism: the belief that the married mother-father-children family is the foundation of society and should be protected and encouraged.

bank.q: Love makes a family; two fathers or two mothers raise children just as well.
bank.ctx: This supports family diversity: the view that same-sex couples and non-traditional families raise children just as well, and that love matters more than family structure.

bank.q: Men and women are naturally suited to different roles, and society works best when it respects that.
bank.ctx: This is a traditional view of gender: that men and women are naturally different and that society works best when its roles reflect those differences.

bank.q: Gender roles are cages built by history, not by biology.
bank.ctx: This is the feminist and progressive view: that differences in men’s and women’s roles come from social conditioning and history rather than nature, and unfairly limit people.

bank.q: Climate change is an existential emergency; our economies must be transformed even at painful cost.
bank.ctx: This treats climate change as an urgent emergency that requires large, even costly, changes to the economy and energy system, and quickly.

bank.q: Climate policy has become a religion of the elites, and working people are the sacrifice.
bank.ctx: This is climate-policy scepticism: the argument that aggressive climate measures are driven by out-of-touch elites and put an unfair burden on ordinary working people.

bank.q: Endless economic growth on a finite planet is a suicide pact.
bank.ctx: This reflects “degrowth” and ecological thinking: that an economy cannot keep growing forever on a planet with limited resources without eventually causing environmental collapse.

bank.q: Growth and innovation, not restraint and rationing, are what actually solve environmental problems.
bank.ctx: This is the eco-modernist view: that continued economic growth and new technology — not cutting back and rationing — are what actually solve environmental problems.

bank.q: Healthcare is a human right and must be free at the point of use for everyone.
bank.ctx: This supports universal public healthcare, like the UK’s NHS: a system funded through taxes and free when you use it, treating medical care as a right for everyone.

bank.q: Government-run healthcare means queues, rationing, and a bureaucrat deciding whether you are worth treating.
bank.ctx: This is the case against fully state-run healthcare: that it leads to long waiting lists, rationed treatment, and officials rather than patients controlling care.

bank.q: Workers create all wealth and deserve far more power over the companies they work for.
bank.ctx: This reflects socialist and trade-union thinking: that workers create a company’s value and therefore should have far more say in how it is run.

bank.q: Unions protect the lazy, strangle businesses, and have driven entire industries into the ground.
bank.ctx: This is the anti-union argument: that organised labour shields unproductive workers, drives up costs, and can push businesses and whole industries into decline.

bank.q: Inherited fortunes entrench a class of people who never earned anything in their lives.
bank.ctx: This argues against large inheritances: that passing down big fortunes creates a privileged class who never earned their wealth, locking inequality in place across generations.

bank.q: Parents have every right to pass on what they built; the state has no claim on a dead person’s life work.
bank.ctx: This defends inheritance: the view that people have the right to leave what they built to their children, and that the state has no claim on it after death (opposing so-called “death taxes”).

bank.q: When everyone gets the same chances, unequal outcomes are just: some people simply work harder.
bank.ctx: This is a meritocratic view: that as long as everyone starts with the same opportunities, differences in wealth are fair because they reflect effort and talent.

bank.q: Equal opportunity is a myth told by the winners; the lottery of birth decides most of who succeeds.
bank.ctx: This challenges the idea of meritocracy: arguing that genuinely equal opportunity does not exist, and that the circumstances you are born into largely decide how far you get.

bank.q: Free trade across open borders has made humanity richer than any other policy in history.
bank.ctx: Free trade means countries buying and selling across borders with few tariffs or barriers. This credits it with raising living standards worldwide more than any other policy.

bank.q: Globalisation gutted our industries and sold out working families to the lowest bidder abroad.
bank.ctx: This is the anti-globalisation argument: that free trade moved factories and jobs to countries with cheaper labour, hollowing out industrial towns and communities at home.

bank.q: Nations must give up some sovereignty to bodies like the UN and EU if humanity is to solve global problems.
bank.ctx: This supports internationalism: the idea that countries must hand some decision-making power to bodies like the UN or EU to tackle problems no single nation can solve alone.

bank.q: No unelected international body should ever be able to override the laws of a sovereign nation.
bank.ctx: This is the sovereigntist position: that no unelected international organisation should ever have the power to overrule the laws of a nation-state.

bank.q: Peace is kept by strength; a nation unwilling to fight will end up ruled by one that is.
bank.ctx: This is the “peace through strength” doctrine: the idea that a country stays safe by being militarily strong and willing to fight, which deters would-be aggressors.

bank.q: Military spending is theft from the hungry; wars enrich arms makers and bury the poor.
bank.ctx: This is the anti-militarist or pacifist view: that money spent on armies and weapons should go to human needs instead, and that wars mainly enrich arms makers.

bank.q: Children should be taught to be proud of their nation’s history, not ashamed of it.
bank.ctx: This supports patriotic education: teaching children to take pride in their country’s history and achievements rather than focusing on its wrongs.

bank.q: A nation that whitewashes its crimes in the classroom is lying to its own children.
bank.ctx: This supports teaching a fuller, more critical history — including crimes such as slavery or colonialism — arguing that glossing over them misleads students.

bank.q: A country of many cultures living side by side is stronger than any monoculture.
bank.ctx: This is the multiculturalist view: that a society made up of many cultures living side by side is richer and stronger than one with a single, uniform culture.

bank.q: Multiculturalism has produced parallel societies that share a passport and nothing else.
bank.ctx: This is the critique of multiculturalism: that instead of integrating, different groups end up living largely separate lives with little in common — so-called “parallel societies.”

bank.q: Some religions are simply incompatible with Western values.
bank.ctx: This argues that certain religions clash with liberal Western values such as free speech and gender equality. In practice the debate usually centres on Islam.

bank.q: Every faith deserves the same freedom and the same respect under the law.
bank.ctx: This is the principle of religious freedom and equality: that every faith deserves the same legal protection and the same respect.

bank.q: Adults own their own bodies; the state has no right to punish anyone for what they choose to consume.
bank.ctx: This is the libertarian view of personal freedom: that adults own their own bodies and have the right to consume what they choose, so the state should not criminalise it.

bank.q: Drug legalisation surrenders the streets to addiction and hands the profits to the cartels.
bank.ctx: This is the case against legalising drugs: that easier access increases addiction and social harm, while the profits still flow to criminal gangs.

bank.q: Sex work is work, and criminalising it only endangers the people who do it.
bank.ctx: This supports decriminalising prostitution: the argument that treating sex work as legitimate work, and regulating it, makes the people who do it safer.

bank.q: Prostitution is paid exploitation, and a decent society does not put a licence on it.
bank.ctx: This opposes legalising prostitution: the view that it is inherently exploitative, especially of vulnerable women, and that a decent society should not give it official approval.

bank.q: Parents, not the state, should decide which values their children are taught.
bank.ctx: This favours parental control over schooling: the idea that parents, not the government or schools, should decide the moral and social values their children are taught.

bank.q: Public schools must teach shared civic values, even when parents object.
bank.ctx: This argues that state schools have a duty to teach shared civic values to all children, even when it conflicts with what some parents want.

bank.q: Complex policy should be decided by scientists and experts, not by politicians chasing votes.
bank.ctx: This is technocracy: the idea that complex issues should be decided by qualified experts rather than by politicians who are influenced by votes and elections.

bank.q: Rule by unelected experts is just tyranny with a diploma.
bank.ctx: This is the populist critique of technocracy: that handing decisions to unelected experts removes democratic accountability and becomes its own kind of tyranny.

bank.q: The mainstream media exists to protect the powerful and manufacture consent.
bank.ctx: This reflects deep distrust of the mainstream press: the view that large media outlets serve elite interests and shape public opinion to benefit the powerful.

bank.q: Independent journalism, whatever its flaws, is a pillar no democracy can stand without.
bank.ctx: This defends the free press: the idea that independent journalism, whatever its faults, is essential for holding those in power to account in a democracy.

bank.q: Governments must force platforms to delete dangerous misinformation.
bank.ctx: This supports government action against false information online, requiring social-media companies to take down content judged dangerous or misleading.

bank.q: Letting the state decide what is true is the end of free thought.
bank.ctx: This warns against government control of information: that letting officials decide what counts as “misinformation” threatens free speech and open debate.

bank.q: Breaking an unjust law is not a crime. It is a duty.
bank.ctx: This is the principle of civil disobedience: the idea that people have a moral duty to break laws they consider deeply unjust, as seen in the civil-rights movement.

bank.q: If everyone obeyed only the laws they personally agree with, civilisation would collapse.
bank.ctx: This defends the rule of law: that society only functions if people obey laws even when they personally disagree, rather than each person picking and choosing.

bank.q: The interests of workers and the interests of owners are fundamentally opposed.
bank.ctx: This is the Marxist idea of class conflict: that employees and business owners have fundamentally opposing interests, since one side’s gain comes at the other’s expense.

bank.q: Employers and employees prosper together; class war is a fantasy that impoverishes both.
bank.ctx: This rejects the idea of class conflict: the view that workers and owners share an interest in a company’s success and both do better when it thrives.

bank.q: As machines replace human work, every citizen must be guaranteed an unconditional basic income.
bank.ctx: Universal basic income (UBI) is a regular, no-strings payment made to every citizen. This supports it as a response to automation and machines replacing human jobs.

bank.q: Paying people to do nothing is the fastest way to destroy the meaning of work.
bank.ctx: This is the argument against a basic income: that paying people whether or not they work removes the incentive and the sense of purpose that come from earning a living.

bank.q: Housing is a right; no one should own ten apartments while families sleep in cars.
bank.ctx: This treats housing as a right and objects to homes being concentrated among investors while others go without — a case for strong government intervention in the housing market.

bank.q: Rent caps and housing mandates have wrecked every housing market they have ever touched.
bank.ctx: This is the economic argument against rent control: that capping rents reduces how much housing gets built or offered, making shortages worse over time.

bank.q: The police need more power and fewer restraints to take back the streets.
bank.ctx: This supports giving the police stronger powers and fewer legal restraints in order to fight crime and restore order on the streets.

bank.q: Hand the police unchecked power and the innocent are always the first casualties.
bank.ctx: This is the civil-liberties argument: that giving police too much unchecked power leads to abuse, and that innocent and marginalised people tend to suffer first.

bank.q: Every young citizen owes their country a period of military or civil service.
bank.ctx: This supports mandatory national service — a set period of military or civilian duty that all young people must complete for their country.

bank.q: The state does not own young people’s lives; conscription is forced labour.
bank.ctx: This opposes compulsory service: the view that forcing young people to serve against their will violates their freedom and amounts to forced labour.

bank.q: Major national decisions should be put directly to the people in referendums.
bank.ctx: This supports direct democracy: putting major national questions straight to the public in referendums rather than leaving them to elected representatives.

bank.q: Referendums reduce complex questions to slogans and mob emotion.
bank.ctx: This is the case against referendums: that complicated issues get reduced to simple yes/no slogans and decided by emotion rather than careful judgement.

bank.q: Traditions carry the accumulated wisdom of generations and should not be discarded lightly.
bank.ctx: This is the conservative view of tradition: that long-standing customs and institutions hold accumulated wisdom, so we should be cautious about sweeping them away.

bank.q: Worship of tradition means letting the dead govern the living.
bank.ctx: This is the progressive reply: that clinging to tradition for its own sake lets the past dictate to the present and blocks change that is needed.

bank.q: People are fundamentally selfish, and any system that pretends otherwise will fail.
bank.ctx: This reflects a pessimistic view of human nature: that people are basically self-interested, so any realistic system must assume selfishness rather than expect generosity.

bank.q: People are fundamentally cooperative; it is unjust systems that make them cruel.
bank.ctx: This reflects an optimistic view of human nature: that people are naturally cooperative, and that it is unjust systems and conditions that bring out cruelty.

heroSub: 100 ideological statements answered on a six-point scale. Every position is asked twice with opposite framing, so your results show where you land, which ideologies you match, and how much wording bends your answers.
